target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is worthwhile because classroom specimens are mostly already deceased and many are meat-industry byproducts.
objection: Even if some specimens are already dead or byproducts, schools still create educational demand for animal bodies. That demand can increase breeding or wild collection in practice, so sourcing claims do not eliminate the ethical and environmental problem.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection offers unique learning value through real anatomical variability and hands-on authenticity.
objection: Good alternatives like 3D models and simulations can teach the same anatomy and variation without using dead animals, sharps, or biohazard disposal. So the authenticity of dissection is not enough to justify it when non-animal methods can cover the same goals.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is a safe and environmentally manageable lab activity if schools use proper protocols.
objection: Proper protocols do not remove the added burdens of hazardous chemicals, biohazard handling, and sharps disposal. Compared with non-animal labs, dissection still produces avoidable safety and environmental harms.

target: AG1’s argument that dissection is justified because the specimens are already-deceased or byproducts and the harms are manageable.
objection: Being a byproduct or already dead is not an ethical justification by itself, because students can learn the same anatomy without using dead animals at all. Also, schools cannot reliably verify that every specimen truly was waste destined for landfill, so the sourcing story is speculative.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection can be made inclusive through opt-out alternatives and separate lab options.
objection: Opt-out does not guarantee true inclusion, because dissection may still be treated as the main or ‘real’ lab and alternatives may be viewed as second-best, creating pressure or stigma for students who choose not to dissect.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is a low-tech, accessible option for schools with limited resources.
objection: Dissection is not necessarily the cheaper or easier long-term option, because it requires recurring specimen procurement, storage, fixatives, PPE, and waste disposal. Reusable non-animal tools and simulations can be more scalable over time.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection uniquely trains students in real scientific practices and lab workflow.
objection: Scientific skills such as observation, measurement, recording, troubleshooting, and safety procedures do not require cutting up animals. Non-animal labs can teach those same competencies without harming animals or producing biohazard waste.

target: AG1’s claim that only dissection can teach real spatial understanding of anatomy in connected tissue.
objection: High-quality 3D models and virtual dissections can teach the same spatial relationships, often better because students can rotate, zoom, relabel, and revisit structures repeatedly instead of relying on one destructive cut. The special tactile feel of real tissue is not enough to justify animal use.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is a distinct, high-value learning method that should not be treated as merely interchangeable with alternatives.
objection: Dissection is often destructive and irreversible, and it can reward cutting technique more than conceptual understanding by obscuring the structures students are meant to study. Because alternatives can preserve visibility and repetition, dissection’s distinctiveness can be a learning disadvantage rather than a benefit.

target: AG1’s claim that good dissection design makes the method educational and therefore justified.
objection: Even well-designed dissection can teach, but that does not answer the ethical standard: if the same curriculum outcomes can be achieved through non-animal methods, then animal dissection remains unnecessary. The harms are avoidable, so educational effectiveness alone is not enough to justify it.
